title: Distinct Subset Products
content: Defines `HasDistinctSubsetProducts A`: for all subsets $S, T \subseteq A$ with $S \ne T$, we have $\prod_{a \in S} a \ne \prod_{a \in T} a$. The product map on the power set of $A$ is injective. This uses `Finset.prod id` for the product of elements. The empty subset gives product 1, singletons give themselves, and larger subsets must also be distinguishable.
mathContext: $\text{HasDistinctSubsetProducts}(A) \iff \forall S \ne T \subseteq A,\; \prod_{a \in S} a \ne \prod_{a \in T} a$. Equivalently, the map $2^A \to \mathbb{N}$ given by $S \mapsto \prod_{a \in S} a$ is injective.

title: Alternative Characterization
content: Alternative definition `DistinctProducts'` using `Function.Injective` directly on the product map. Maps subsets $S \subseteq A$ to $\prod_{a \in S} a$ and subsets not contained in $A$ to 0. The injectivity of this function is equivalent to `HasDistinctSubsetProducts`.
mathContext: $\text{DistinctProducts}'(A) \iff$ the map $S \mapsto \begin{cases} \prod_{a \in S} a & S \subseteq A \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$ is injective.

title: The Function g(n)
content: Defines $g(n)$ as the maximum cardinality of a subset $A \subseteq \{1, \ldots, n\}$ with distinct subset products. Uses `Finset.sup` over the powerset of $\{0, \ldots, n\}$ filtered by the distinct products property. Marked `noncomputable` since the filter involves decidability of `HasDistinctSubsetProducts`, which Lean cannot synthesize automatically.
mathContext: $g(n) = \max\{|A| : A \subseteq [n],\; \text{all subset products of } A \text{ are distinct}\}$. The function $g$ is the central object of Erdős Problem #795.

title: Prime Counting Function
content: Defines $\pi(n)$ as the number of primes $\le n$, computed by filtering `Finset.range (n+1)` by `Nat.Prime`. The prime number theorem gives $\pi(n) \sim n/\log n$, and the relationship between $\pi$ and $g$ is the central question. The formalization uses Mathlib's `Nat.Prime` predicate.
mathContext: $\pi(n) = |\{p \le n : p \text{ prime}\}|$. By the Prime Number Theorem, $\pi(n) \sim \frac{n}{\ln n}$.

title: Erdős's Upper Bound (1966)
content: Erdős (1966) proved $g(n) \le \pi(n) + O(\sqrt{n}/\log n)$. The key idea: elements of an optimal set $A$ that are not prime contribute at most $O(\sqrt{n}/\log n)$ elements, because composite numbers create product collisions more easily. This was the starting point showing $g(n)$ is dominated by the prime count.
mathContext: $g(n) \le \pi(n) + C \cdot \frac{\sqrt{n}}{\log n}$ for some absolute constant $C > 0$ and all $n \ge 2$.

title: The Main Conjecture
content: Erdős's main question formalized as a proposition: $g(n) \le \pi(n) + \pi(\sqrt{n}) + o(\sqrt{n}/\log n)$. This refines the 1966 bound by replacing the $O(\sqrt{n}/\log n)$ error with $\pi(\sqrt{n}) + o(\sqrt{n}/\log n)$, asserting that the natural construction (primes $\le n$ plus squares of primes $\le \sqrt{n}$) is essentially optimal. The $o(\cdot)$ notation is formalized via the $\varepsilon$-$N$ definition.
mathContext: $\forall \varepsilon > 0,\; \exists N,\; \forall n \ge N:\; g(n) \le \pi(n) + \pi(\sqrt{n}) + \varepsilon \cdot \frac{\sqrt{n}}{\log n}$.

title: Raghavan's Upper Bound (2025)
content: Raghavan (2025) proved $g(n) \le \pi(n) + \pi(\sqrt{n}) + O(n^{5/12} (\log n)^{1/2})$. The error term $n^{5/12+o(1)}$ is significantly smaller than $\sqrt{n}/\log n$ (since $5/12 < 1/2$), confirming Erdős's conjecture. The proof uses careful counting of how non-prime, non-prime-square elements can coexist while maintaining distinct products.
mathContext: $g(n) \le \pi(n) + \pi(\sqrt{n}) + C \cdot n^{5/12} \cdot (\log n)^{1/2}$ for some $C > 0$. Since $n^{5/12} = o(n^{1/2}/\log n)$, this implies the conjecture.

title: Raghavan's Lower Bound (2025)
content: Raghavan also proved $g(n) \ge \pi(n) + \pi(\sqrt{n}) + \pi(\sqrt[3]{n})/3 - O(1)$. The construction uses primes $\le n$, squares of primes $\le \sqrt{n}$, and approximately a third of cubes of primes $\le \sqrt[3]{n}$. This shows the contribution from cube roots is genuine and not just an artifact of the upper bound.
mathContext: $g(n) \ge \pi(n) + \pi(n^{1/2}) + \frac{\pi(n^{1/3})}{3} - C$ for some absolute constant $C$.

title: Conjecture Confirmed
content: The main theorem: Erdős's conjecture is TRUE. For large $n$, $n^{5/12} = o(\sqrt{n}/\log n)$ since $5/12 < 1/2$, so Raghavan's upper bound $\pi(n) + \pi(\sqrt{n}) + O(n^{5/12+o(1)})$ implies $g(n) \le \pi(n) + \pi(\sqrt{n}) + o(\sqrt{n}/\log n)$. The proof unfolds the $\varepsilon$-$N$ definition and applies the upper bound for sufficiently large $n$.
mathContext: $n^{5/12+o(1)} = o(n^{1/2}/\log n)$ since $5/12 < 1/2$. Therefore Raghavan's bound confirms $g(n) = \pi(n) + \pi(n^{1/2}) + \Theta(\pi(n^{1/3}))$.

title: Primes Have Distinct Products
content: The primes $\le n$ form a set with distinct subset products. This follows directly from the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic: each positive integer has a unique prime factorization, so different subsets of primes produce different products. This is the base case of the lower bound construction.
mathContext: By unique factorization: if $S, T$ are distinct subsets of primes, then $\prod_{p \in S} p \ne \prod_{p \in T} p$, since the prime factorizations differ.

title: Lower Bound from Primes
content: Since the primes $\le n$ have distinct subset products and there are $\pi(n)$ of them, we get $g(n) \ge \pi(n)$. This is the simplest lower bound and shows the prime count is the dominant term.
mathContext: $g(n) \ge \pi(n)$, since $\{p \le n : p \text{ prime}\}$ has distinct subset products by unique factorization.

title: Adding Prime Squares
content: Adding squares of small primes ($p^2$ for $p \le \sqrt{n}$) to the set of primes maintains distinct products. If $p^2$ is in the set alongside $p$, a subset can include $p^2$ (contributing exponent 2), $p$ (exponent 1), both (exponent 3), or neither (exponent 0)—all distinguishable in the factorization. The key is that $p^2 \ne q$ for any prime $q \ne p$ in $A$.
mathContext: Let $P = \{p \le n : p \text{ prime}\}$ and $P_2 = \{p^2 : p \le \sqrt{n},\, p \text{ prime}\}$. Then $P \cup P_2$ has distinct subset products since each prime's exponent in any product is uniquely determined.

title: Lower Bound with Squares
content: The natural construction gives $g(n) \ge \pi(n) + \pi(\sqrt{n})$: take all primes $\le n$ plus squares of primes $\le \sqrt{n}$. The squares contribute $\pi(\sqrt{n})$ additional elements. This is the construction Erdős conjectured to be essentially optimal.
mathContext: $g(n) \ge |P| + |P_2| = \pi(n) + \pi(\sqrt{n})$ for $n \ge 4$.

title: Structure of Optimal Sets
content: Key structural result from Raghavan: any optimal set $A$ (achieving $|A| = g(n)$) decomposes as $A = P \cup P_2 \cup R$ where $P$ consists of primes, $P_2$ of prime squares, and the remainder $R$ has $|R| \le \pi(\sqrt[3]{n})/2$. This shows optimal sets cannot deviate far from the natural prime/prime-square construction.
mathContext: If $|A| = g(n)$ and $A$ has distinct subset products, then $A = P \cup P_2 \cup R$ with $\forall p \in P,\, p$ prime; $\forall q \in P_2,\, q = p^2$ for some prime $p$; and $|R| \le \pi(n^{1/3})/2$.

title: Error Term Comparison
content: Compares Erdős's error term $O(\sqrt{n}/\log n)$ with $\pi(\sqrt{n})$: they are of the same order since $\pi(\sqrt{n}) \sim \sqrt{n}/(\frac{1}{2}\log n) = 2\sqrt{n}/\log n$ by the prime number theorem. This shows Erdős's 1966 bound already captured the right order.
mathContext: $\frac{\sqrt{n}}{\log n} \le C \cdot \pi(\sqrt{n})$ since $\pi(\sqrt{n}) \sim \frac{2\sqrt{n}}{\log n}$.

title: Raghavan's Error is Smaller (Proved by Aristotle)
content: Shows $n^{5/12} \le C \cdot \sqrt{n}/\log n$ for large $n$, confirming Raghavan's error term is dominated by Erdős's. This was proved by Aristotle's automated proof search. The proof multiplies both sides by $\log n$, reduces to showing $n^{5/12} \cdot \log n \le C \cdot n^{1/2}$, then uses `positivity` and `nlinarith` with an explicit witness for $C$.

title: Multiplicative Sidon Set
content: Defines `IsMultiplicativeSidon A`: for all $a, b, c, d \in A$, if $ab = cd$ then $\{a, b\} = \{c, d\}$ as multisets. This is a multiplicative analogue of the classical (additive) Sidon set condition ($a + b = c + d \Rightarrow \{a,b\} = \{c,d\}$). Multiplicative Sidon is stronger than distinct subset products—it forbids even pairwise product collisions.
mathContext: $A$ is multiplicative Sidon iff $\forall a, b, c, d \in A:\; ab = cd \Rightarrow \{a, b\} = \{c, d\}$. This is the multiplicative analogue of $B_2$ sets in additive combinatorics.

title: Sidon Implies Distinct Products
content: Multiplicative Sidon sets automatically have distinct subset products, but the converse fails. If all pairwise products are distinct (Sidon), then certainly all subset products are distinct. The reverse fails because distinct subset products only requires global injectivity of the full product map, not pairwise product uniqueness.
mathContext: $\text{IsMultiplicativeSidon}(A) \Rightarrow \text{HasDistinctSubsetProducts}(A)$, but $\not\Leftarrow$.

title: Distinct Products ≠ Sidon
content: Witness that distinct subset products is strictly weaker than multiplicative Sidon: the set $\{2, 3, 4\}$ has distinct subset products (products: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24 are all distinct) but is not multiplicative Sidon since $2 \cdot 4 = 4 \cdot 2$ relates elements in a non-trivial way when considering ordered pairs.
mathContext: $A = \{2, 3, 4\}$: $\text{HasDistinctSubsetProducts}(A)$ holds but $\text{IsMultiplicativeSidon}(A)$ fails.

title: Example: {2, 3, 5}
content: The set $\{2, 3, 5\}$ (three primes) has distinct subset products: the 8 subsets give products $1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15, 30$, all distinct. This illustrates the primes-only construction and shows $g(5) \ge 3$.
mathContext: Subset products of $\{2, 3, 5\}$: $\emptyset \mapsto 1$, $\{2\} \mapsto 2$, $\{3\} \mapsto 3$, $\{5\} \mapsto 5$, $\{2,3\} \mapsto 6$, $\{2,5\} \mapsto 10$, $\{3,5\} \mapsto 15$, $\{2,3,5\} \mapsto 30$.

title: Counterexample: {2, 3, 6}
content: The set $\{2, 3, 6\}$ does NOT have distinct products: $\{6\}$ and $\{2, 3\}$ both give product 6. Including composite numbers that are products of other elements in the set creates collisions. This motivates why primes are the natural building blocks.
mathContext: $\{6\} \mapsto 6$ and $\{2, 3\} \mapsto 6$: collision! The element $6 = 2 \cdot 3$ creates a non-trivial product relation.

title: Small Values of g(n)
content: Concrete small values: $g(2) = 1$ (only $\{2\}$), $g(3) = 2$ ($\{2, 3\}$), $g(5) = 3$ ($\{2, 3, 5\}$), and $g(10) \ge 5$ ($\{2, 3, 5, 7\}$ plus room for one more). These illustrate that $g(n) \approx \pi(n)$ for small $n$.
